questions.question: Article 51 of the Indian constitution is related with which of the following?

options.text: Promotion of international peace and security
Organization of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Promotion of international peace and security**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 51** of the **Indian Constitution** falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV).
 
• Its primary objective is the **promotion of international peace and security**, ensuring harmony between nations.
 
• This article explicitly outlines the role of India in fostering **respect for international law and treaty obligations** in dealings with organized nations.
 
• It emphasizes maintaining a just and equitable **global order** and encourages peaceful coexistence among countries.
 
• Article 51 is not enforceable by the courts but serves as a guiding principle for the government in formulating policies and decisions at the international level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSPs are enumerated in **Part IV** of the Indian Constitution and are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
• They are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by the courts, but they act as guidelines for the government to create laws and policies.
 
• Examples include **Article 44** (Uniform Civil Code), **Article 48** (Organization of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry), etc.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Article 51:**
 
 
• It directs the state to work for the **promotion of international peace and security**.
 
• Urges maintaining **friendly relations** with other countries.
 
• Encourages respect for **international law** and treaty obligations.
 
• Promotes the resolution of disputes by **arbitration** instead of conflict.
 
 
 
• **Relation to India’s Foreign Policy:**
 
 
• Article 51 aligns with India's vision of **non-alignment** and peaceful coexistence as propagated by leaders like **Jawaharlal Nehru**.
 
• It is reflected in various international initiatives, including India's role in the **United Nations** and its emphasis on **disarmament** and **global cooperation**.
 
• India’s commitment to treaties like the **Paris Climate Agreement** and active participation in **peacekeeping missions** showcase adherence to Article 51.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Implementation:**
 
 
• India has supported global peace initiatives and participated in **United Nations peacekeeping missions**.
 
• It has advocated for nuclear disarmament and signed treaties promoting **global security**.
 
• India’s foreign policy often reflects respect for international law and the resolution of disputes through peaceful means.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Article 44:** Relates to the **Uniform Civil Code**, aiming to unify personal laws across all religions in India.
 
• **Article 48:** Deals with the **organization of agriculture and animal husbandry**, promoting scientific methods and the prohibition of slaughter of certain animals.
 
• **Article 43:** Encourages the **promotion of cooperative societies** for economic development.
 
• These articles reflect the broader goals of the Directive Principles in ensuring equitable development and social justice.

• **Anurag Garg** was appointed as the **Director General** of the **Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB)** in **September 2024**.

• Anurag Garg is a senior officer with vast experience in administrative and enforcement roles, making him suitable for this crucial position.
 
• The appointment comes at a time when the **NCB** is focusing on dismantling drug networks and addressing rising drug abuse cases in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB):**

 
 
• The **NCB** was established in **1986** under the **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985**.
 
• Its primary function is to coordinate with various states and international agencies to curb drug trafficking.
 
• The agency works under the administrative control of the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, Government of India.
 
• The **NCB** also monitors India's compliance with international drug control treaties and conventions.
 
 
 
• **Key Functions of NCB:**
 
 
• Investigating and prosecuting offenses related to narcotics and psychotropic substances.
 
• Coordinating between central and state agencies to strengthen anti-drug efforts.
 
• Providing training and resources to law enforcement agencies for better drug crime management.
 
• Promoting public awareness campaigns to reduce drug abuse in society.
 
 
 
• **Anurag Garg's Background:**
 
 
• Anurag Garg is a highly experienced officer with expertise in enforcement and administrative processes.
 
• He has held several senior positions in government and law enforcement agencies, contributing to the development of effective policies.
 
• His leadership is expected to address the challenges in drug trafficking and misuse comprehensively.
 
 
 
• **India's Drug Problem:**
 
 
• India faces significant challenges with drug trafficking due to its geographical proximity to the "Golden Triangle" and "Golden Crescent" regions.
 
• Rising substance abuse cases have made it imperative for agencies like NCB to adopt proactive measures.
 
• NCB's role in coordinating efforts at the national and international level is crucial in curbing this menace.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **International Collaboration:**

 
 
• NCB partners with agencies like the **United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC)**, **Interpol**, and **World Customs Organization** to combat drug trafficking.
 
• India is a signatory to several international treaties, such as the **Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961**, and the **United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988**.
 
 
 
• **Drug Awareness and Prevention:**
 
 
• NCB conducts awareness campaigns targeting schools, colleges, and communities to educate people about the dangers of drug abuse.
 
• Effective rehabilitation programs are promoted to help individuals recover from addiction.

questions.question: On October 2, 2024, the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan was launched in ______.
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan** was launched on **October 2, 2024**, in the state of **Jharkhand**.
 
• This initiative focuses on the development and empowerment of **tribal communities** residing in rural areas of the state.
 
• The name **“Dharti Aaba”** is a tribute to **Birsa Munda**, a prominent tribal freedom fighter and social reformer from Jharkhand.
 
• The program aims to enhance the livelihood, education, and health facilities of tribal communities, ensuring inclusive growth and sustainable development.
 
• **Jharkhand**, being rich in tribal heritage and culture, is a key region for such initiatives that target the socio-economic upliftment of marginalized communities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jharkhand:**

 
 
• It is located in eastern India and was formed on **November 15, 2000**, carved out of **Bihar**.
 
• The state is known for its **tribal population**, which constitutes a significant part of its demographic composition.
 
• Prominent tribes include **Santals, Oraons, Mundas, and Hos**.
 
• Jharkhand is rich in **natural resources**, including minerals like coal, iron ore, and mica, which contribute significantly to its economy.
 
 
 
• **Birsa Munda:**
 
 
• Birsa Munda is a revered tribal leader, often referred to as **“Dharti Aaba,”** meaning “Father of the Earth.”
 
• He led a tribal uprising against British colonial rule during the late 19th century in the Chotanagpur region.
 
• Birsa Munda fought for the rights and dignity of tribal communities, emphasizing the importance of land ownership and cultural preservation.
 
• His birth anniversary, **November 15**, is celebrated as **Jharkhand Foundation Day** and Tribal Pride Day in India.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Development Programs:**
 
 
• Numerous government initiatives are aimed at improving the socio-economic conditions of tribal communities, such as the **Vanbandhu Kalyan Yojana** and **Tribal Sub-Plan**.
 
• These programs focus on areas like education, healthcare, infrastructure, and livelihood opportunities for tribal populations.
 
• Special attention is given to preserving tribal culture and traditions while ensuring access to modern amenities.
 
 
 
• **October 2 Significance:**
 
 
• **October 2** is celebrated as **Gandhi Jayanti**, marking the birth anniversary of **Mahatma Gandhi**, the Father of the Nation.
 
• It is also recognized as the **International Day of Non-Violence** by the United Nations.
 
• Launching a tribal development initiative on this date underscores the values of **inclusivity, equality, and social justice** that Mahatma Gandhi advocated.

questions.question: The Allographa effusosoredica, a newly discovered species in western ghats belong to ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**lichen**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Allographa effusosoredica** is a newly discovered species that belongs to the group of **lichens**.
 
• **Lichens** are symbiotic associations between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium, which work together to survive in various environments.
 
• This species was recently discovered in the **Western Ghats of India**, a biodiversity hotspot known for its rich and unique flora and fauna.
 
• The study and discovery of new lichen species like **Allographa effusosoredica** contribute significantly to understanding ecosystem dynamics and biodiversity.
 
• Lichens are considered excellent **bioindicators** of environmental health as they are sensitive to pollution and changes in their habitat.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About Lichens:**

 
 
• Lichens are composed of two organisms: a **fungus** (mycobiont) and a photosynthetic partner, which could be an **alga or cyanobacterium** (photobiont).
 
• They are found in diverse habitats, from arctic tundras to tropical rainforests, and even in extreme environments like deserts.
 
• Lichens play a crucial role in the ecosystem by contributing to **soil formation** and serving as a food source for various animals.
 
 
 
• **Western Ghats:**
 
 
• The **Western Ghats**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is one of the eight "hottest hotspots" of biological diversity in the world.
 
• It spans the states of **Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, and Gujarat**.
 
• This region is home to a large number of endemic species, including plants, animals, and fungi, and is a vital area for new species discoveries.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Lichens:**
 
 
• Lichens are used as **bioindicators** to monitor air pollution, as they are highly sensitive to pollutants like sulfur dioxide.
 
• They are also used in traditional medicines and dyes. For instance, some species produce unique compounds with **antibacterial** and **antiviral properties**.
 
• In addition, lichens contribute to **carbon cycling** in ecosystems by fixing atmospheric carbon dioxide.
 
 
 
• **Other Options Explained:**
 
 
• **Cat:** A domesticated mammal belonging to the family **Felidae**, with no relation to lichens or the species in question.
 
• **Bat:** A mammal capable of sustained flight, belonging to the order **Chiroptera**. It is not related to the discovery of **Allographa effusosoredica**.
 
• **Butterfly:** An insect belonging to the order **Lepidoptera**, known for its colorful wings and unrelated to lichens.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Scientific Research:** The discovery of **Allographa effusosoredica** highlights the importance of systematic research in unexplored or under-researched regions like the **Western Ghats**.
 
• **Conservation:** Understanding lichen diversity is critical for **conservation strategies**, as these organisms are sensitive to environmental changes and can indicate ecological health.
 
• **Global Significance:** India’s biodiversity, especially in hotspots like the Western Ghats, is significant for global ecological balance and sustainability efforts.

questions.question: ’Mangal’ folk songs are traditional to which Indian state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttarakhand**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **‘Mangal’ folk songs** are deeply rooted in the cultural traditions of **Uttarakhand**, a northern Indian state known for its Himalayan beauty and cultural richness.
 
• These songs are traditionally sung during **auspicious occasions** such as weddings, childbirth celebrations, and other ceremonies to invoke blessings and celebrate the event.
 
• The themes of these songs revolve around **devotional, spiritual, and cultural aspects**, often praising deities, especially local gods and goddesses, and describing the beauty of nature and human relationships.
 
• The folk songs are performed in the **Garhwali and Kumaoni languages**, which are the primary dialects of the people of Uttarakhand.
 
• ‘Mangal’ songs are usually sung in a group, accompanied by traditional musical instruments like the **dholak, damau, and harmonium**, which add rhythm and vibrancy to the performances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Uttarakhand Culture:**

 
 
• **Uttarakhand**, also known as **Devbhoomi** (Land of Gods), is famous for its **rich cultural heritage**, including folk music, dance, and art forms.
 
• The state has two main cultural regions: **Garhwal** and **Kumaon**, both of which contribute significantly to its folk traditions.
 
• Traditional festivals like **Harela, Basant Panchami, and Ghee Sankranti** are celebrated with folk songs and dances.
 
 
 
• **Garhwali and Kumaoni Folk Music:**
 
 
• Garhwali and Kumaoni music forms the backbone of Uttarakhand's folk culture, with songs like **Jhoda, Chhopati, and Mangal**.
 
• These songs are often performed during **festivals, social gatherings, and life events**, reflecting the region’s **natural beauty, mythology, and daily life**.
 
 
 
• **Traditional Musical Instruments:**
 
 
• Instruments such as **dhol, damau, turri, and ransingha** are integral to Uttarakhand’s musical tradition.
 
• These instruments are used to accompany folk songs, creating a **distinctive rhythmic pattern** that enhances the overall performance.
 
 
 
• **Significance of ‘Mangal’ Songs:**
 
 
• ‘Mangal’ songs are considered **auspicious** and are an essential part of ceremonies in Uttarakhand.
 
• These songs are believed to invoke the **blessings of deities** and ensure prosperity and happiness for the family.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Folk Traditions in Uttarakhand:**

 
 
• **Jagar:** A ritual song performed to evoke deities or spirits, often used in healing ceremonies.
 
• **Chhopati:** Romantic folk songs sung as duets by men and women.
 
• **Jhoda:** Group songs sung during festivals and fairs, often accompanied by dance.

questions.question: ’Pinjar’, a book portraying the trauma of Partition has been written by which Indian author?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Amrita Pritam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Amrita Pritam** is one of the most celebrated authors of Indian literature, especially in Punjabi and Hindi.
 
• She is known for her poignant works that explore themes of **love, loss, and the trauma of Partition**.
 
• **Pinjar**, published in **1950**, is her most iconic novel and portrays the struggles of women during the **Partition of India** in 1947.
 
• The story revolves around a young woman, Puro, who is abducted and faces challenges that reflect the **deep scars left by Partition**.
 
• Amrita Pritam became the first woman to win the prestigious **Sahitya Akademi Award** in **1956** for her work "Sunehade."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Amrita Pritam:**

 
 
• She was born on **31 August 1919** in Gujranwala, Punjab (now in Pakistan).
 
• She wrote extensively in both **Punjabi** and **Hindi** languages.
 
• Her career spanned over six decades, and she authored more than **100 books**, including poetry, fiction, biographies, essays, and folk songs.
 
• She received the **Padma Shri** in **1969** and the **Padma Vibhushan** in **2004**.
 
• She was honored with the **Jnanpith Award** in **1982**, India's highest literary award.
 
 
 
• **Partition of India:**
 
 
• The **Partition of India** in **1947** divided British India into two independent dominions: **India** and **Pakistan**.
 
• This led to one of the largest migrations in human history, with an estimated **10-15 million people** displaced.
 
• It caused widespread violence, including riots, massacres, and atrocities, leaving a deep impact on the socio-political fabric of the region.
 
 
 
• **Pinjar:**
 
 
• The novel **Pinjar** is a powerful depiction of the social and psychological consequences of Partition.
 
• It highlights the plight of women, who were often victims of abduction, forced marriages, and societal rejection during this tumultuous period.
 
• The book was later adapted into a **Bollywood movie** in **2003**, directed by **Chandra Prakash Dwivedi**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Authors:**
 
 
• **Krishna Sobti:** Known for her contributions to Hindi literature, but not related to "Pinjar."
 
• **Ismat Chughtai:** Famous for her Urdu writings and bold themes, but did not write "Pinjar."
 
• **Mahadevi Verma:** Renowned as a Hindi poet and a major figure in Chhayavaad poetry, her works differ from the themes of "Pinjar."
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Amrita Pritam's Legacy:**

 
 
• She remains an inspiration for her fearless exploration of themes like **love, feminism, and social justice**.
 
• Her poem "**Ajj Aakhaan Waris Shah Nu**" is a famous lament for the bloodshed during Partition.
 
• Her autobiographical works, such as "**Rasidi Ticket**," provide insight into her personal and professional life.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Partition on Literature:**
 
 
• The Partition inspired numerous writers to document its horrors, including **Sadat Hasan Manto**, **Khushwant Singh**, and **Bapsi Sidhwa**.
 
• Literature from this period often deals with themes of identity, loss, communal tensions, and resilience.

questions.question: Which of the following is a traditional dance associated with the culture of Sikkim?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Snow Lion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Snow Lion dance** is a traditional dance of **Sikkim**, performed during cultural and religious occasions in the region.
 
• This dance is deeply rooted in the **Buddhist tradition** of the state and is part of the rituals and festivities in monasteries.
 
• The Snow Lion symbolizes **strength, fearlessness, and joy**, representing the protector deity of the mountains in Tibetan Buddhism.
 
• Performers wear elaborate costumes resembling a lion, and the dance is accompanied by **traditional musical instruments** like drums and cymbals.
 
• It is often performed during **Losar celebrations** (Tibetan New Year) and other important festivals, highlighting the rich cultural heritage of Sikkim.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Loor Dance:**

 
 
• **Origin:** The Loor dance belongs to **Haryana** and is performed by women during the spring season.
 
• **Theme:** It is a folk dance that narrates tales of love and marriage.
 
• **Performance:** Dancers dress in bright traditional attire and perform with rhythmic movements.
 
 
 
• **Dindi Dance:**
 
 
• **Origin:** The Dindi dance is associated with **Maharashtra**, performed during religious gatherings.
 
• **Theme:** It represents devotion towards Lord Krishna and features devotional songs.
 
• **Performance:** Dancers move in a circular formation, accompanied by cymbals and drums.
 
 
 
• **Padhar Dance:**
 
 
• **Origin:** The Padhar dance is a folk tradition of the **Gujarat** region.
 
• **Theme:** It is performed by the Padhar community to depict their lifestyle and relationship with water.
 
• **Performance:** Participants wear colorful attire and perform near water bodies.
 
 
 
• **Snow Lion Dance:**
 
 
• **Origin:** This dance is specific to **Sikkim** and the Himalayan region, rooted in **Tibetan Buddhist culture**.
 
• **Symbolism:** The Snow Lion is a mythical creature representing strength, wisdom, and protection.
 
• **Performance:** It is often showcased during **Losar** and other ceremonial events with performers wearing lion costumes and masks.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Sikkim:**

 
 
• **Location:** Sikkim is a northeastern state of India bordered by Bhutan, Nepal, and Tibet.

questions.question: The most popular argument regarding the origin of the universe is the _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Big Bang Theory**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Big Bang Theory** is the most widely accepted explanation for the origin of the universe. It proposes that the universe began approximately **13.8 billion years ago** from an extremely hot and dense singularity.
 
• The theory states that the universe expanded rapidly from this singularity, leading to the formation of matter, energy, space, and time.
 
• **Edwin Hubble's observations** in the 1920s provided the first evidence for the Big Bang Theory. He discovered that galaxies are moving away from each other, which implies the universe is expanding.
 
• The presence of the **cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB)**, discovered in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, supports the theory. This radiation is the remnant heat from the initial explosion.
 
• The theory also explains the abundance of light elements such as **hydrogen and helium**, which were formed during the first few minutes after the Big Bang.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Plate Tectonics**:

 
 
• Plate tectonics is a geological theory explaining the movement of Earth's lithospheric plates. It is unrelated to the origin of the universe.
 
• This theory helps explain phenomena such as **earthquakes, volcanic activity, and the formation of mountains.**
 
• It was developed in the 20th century based on evidence from **continental drift, seafloor spreading, and fossil records.**
 
 
 
• **Quantum Mechanics**:
 
 
• Quantum mechanics is a branch of physics that deals with the behavior of particles at atomic and subatomic levels.
 
• While it provides insights into the fundamental nature of matter and energy, it does not directly address the origin of the universe.
 
 
 
• **String Theory**:
 
 
• String theory is a theoretical framework in physics that attempts to unify all fundamental forces, including gravity, using one-dimensional strings.
 
• It is a potential candidate for explaining the universe's fundamental structure but remains speculative and does not directly explain the origin of the universe.
 
 
 
• **Key Scientists and Discoveries:**
 
 
• **Georges Lemaître**, a Belgian astronomer and physicist, first proposed the idea of a universe originating from a "primordial atom," now known as the Big Bang Theory.
 
• **Edwin Hubble** provided observational evidence of an expanding universe through the **redshift** of galaxies.
 
• **Robert Wilson** and **Arno Penzias** discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation, further validating the theory.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMB):** The CMB is considered the "afterglow" of the Big Bang and provides strong evidence for the theory. It was discovered in **1964** and has been studied extensively using satellites such as **COBE, WMAP, and Planck.**
 
• **Expanding Universe:** Observations of galaxies moving away from each other indicate that the universe is expanding. This phenomenon is described by the **Hubble Law**, which states that the velocity of a galaxy is proportional to its distance from us.
 
• **Light Element Formation:** The Big Bang Theory predicts the abundance of light elements such as **hydrogen** (75%) and **helium** (25%), formed during the process known as **Big Bang Nucleosynthesis.**
 
• **Future Research:** Scientists continue to study the universe's origin using advanced telescopes like the **James Webb Space Telescope** and gravitational wave observatories.

questions.question: In the late 1980s, the government of India approached an International Bank for Reconstruction and Development to tackle with the economic crisis, that bank is also known as _________.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the late **1980s**, India faced a severe **economic crisis**, characterized by balance of payment issues, high fiscal deficits, and declining foreign exchange reserves.
 
• The Government of India approached the **International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)**, commonly known as the **World Bank**, to seek assistance in stabilizing its economy and addressing structural inefficiencies.
 
• The **World Bank** is an international financial institution established in **1944** to provide financial and technical assistance to developing countries worldwide.
 
• The World Bank played a crucial role in designing and implementing structural reforms in India during this period, focusing on liberalization, privatization, and globalization policies.
 
• The assistance provided by the World Bank marked a shift in India's economic policy towards a more open and market-oriented economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **World Bank:**

 
 
• Established in **1944**, the World Bank is headquartered in **Washington, D.C., USA**.
 
• It comprises five institutions, including the **IBRD** and the **International Development Association (IDA)**.
 
• The primary aim is to provide **long-term loans** and financial assistance to developing countries for developmental projects such as infrastructure, health, and education.
 
• India has been one of the largest borrowers from the World Bank, focusing on infrastructure, rural development, and poverty alleviation projects.
 
 
 
• **Asian Development Bank (ADB):**
 
 
• Founded in **1966**, the ADB is headquartered in **Mandaluyong, Philippines**.
 
• Its primary focus is on promoting social and economic development in the Asia-Pacific region.
 
• Unlike the World Bank, ADB has a regional focus and provides financial assistance primarily to countries in Asia.
 
 
 
• **World Trade Bank:**
 
 
• No such institution as "World Trade Bank" exists; the term might be mistakenly used to refer to the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**.
 
• The WTO focuses on international trade rules and regulations, promoting free trade, and resolving trade disputes.
 
 
 
• **Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB):**
 
 
• Established in **2016**, the AIIB is headquartered in **Beijing, China**.
 
• It focuses on financing infrastructure projects in Asia and beyond, such as transportation, energy, and urban development.
 
• India is one of the largest borrowers from the AIIB, with funds directed towards projects like metro development and renewable energy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **World Bank** differs from regional financial institutions like the **Asian Development Bank (ADB)** and the **Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)**, as it operates globally and focuses on broader developmental goals.
 
• The **economic reforms** initiated in India during the late 1980s and early 1990s, under the guidance of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), are referred to as the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) reforms**.
 
• The World Bank's involvement during this period played a pivotal role in reshaping India's economic trajectory and integrating it into the global economy.

questions.question: Which Sikh Guru instituted the Khalsa in 1699?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Guru Gobind Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Guru Gobind Singh**, the tenth Sikh Guru, established the **Khalsa** on **13 April 1699**, which coincides with the festival of **Baisakhi**.
 
• The **Khalsa** was created to instill a sense of unity, courage, and justice among Sikhs and to prepare them to defend their faith against oppression.
 
• The initiation ceremony, known as **Amrit Sanchar**, was conducted at **Anandpur Sahib**, where Guru Gobind Singh baptized the first five Sikhs, known as the **Panj Pyare** (Five Beloved Ones).
 
• The creation of the Khalsa marked a turning point in Sikh history, transforming Sikhs into a community of saint-soldiers committed to protecting the oppressed and upholding justice.
 
• The Khalsa was guided by strict principles, including the adoption of the **Five Ks** (Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kirpan, and Kachera), which became the identity symbols of the Sikhs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Guru Gobind Singh**:

 
 
• Born on **22 December 1666**, Guru Gobind Singh was the last of the ten Sikh Gurus.
 
• He was a spiritual leader, poet, philosopher, and warrior who dedicated his life to the principles of justice and equality.
 
• Guru Gobind Singh compiled the **Dasam Granth** and declared the **Guru Granth Sahib** as the eternal Guru of the Sikhs.
 
 
 
• **The Panj Pyare**:
 
 
• The **Panj Pyare** were the first five Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa. Their names were **Bhai Daya Singh, Bhai Dharam Singh, Bhai Himmat Singh, Bhai Mohkam Singh,** and **Bhai Sahib Singh**.
 
• They voluntarily offered their lives to Guru Gobind Singh during the Khalsa initiation ceremony, symbolizing courage and self-sacrifice.
 
 
 
• **The Five Ks**:
 
 
• The Five Ks are the five articles of faith that every baptized Sikh is required to wear:
 
 
• **Kesh**: Uncut hair, symbolizing spirituality and respect for God’s creation.
 
• **Kangha**: A wooden comb, representing cleanliness and order.
 
• **Kara**: A steel bracelet, signifying restraint and responsibility.
 
• **Kirpan**: A ceremonial sword, symbolizing the duty to protect the weak and uphold justice.
 
• **Kachera**: Cotton undergarments, representing self-discipline and modesty.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Anandpur Sahib**:
 
 
• Located in modern-day Punjab, Anandpur Sahib is one of the holiest places in Sikhism and the site where the Khalsa was established.
 
• It is also home to the **Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib**, one of the five temporal seats of authority in Sikhism.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Khalsa:**
 
 
• The Khalsa emphasizes qualities such as courage, discipline, equality, and selflessness.
 
• It played a crucial role in defending Sikhism and other oppressed communities during times of persecution.
 
• The Khalsa continues to represent the core values of Sikhism, uniting Sikhs worldwide under a shared identity.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Guru Nanak**: The founder of Sikhism and the first Sikh Guru, he emphasized the oneness of God and equality of all beings.
 
• **Guru Ram Das**: The fourth Sikh Guru, credited with founding the city of **Amritsar** and establishing the spiritual and social institutions of Sikhism.
 
• **Guru Tegh Bahadur**: The ninth Sikh Guru, who sacrificed his life to protect religious freedom and the rights of the oppressed.
 
• **Guru Gobind Singh**: The initiator of the Khalsa, he contributed significantly to the spiritual, social, and military aspects of Sikhism, ensuring its survival against external threats.

• The slogan **"Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!"** was given by **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** during the Indian freedom struggle. This slogan became a rallying cry for Indians fighting for independence.
 
• Tilak used this slogan to instill a sense of pride and urgency among Indians and encourage them to actively participate in the freedom movement.
 
• It was during the **1906 Congress session** that Tilak popularized this slogan, emphasizing the need for Swaraj (self-rule) for India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Legacy of the Slogan:**
 
 
• "Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!" continues to symbolize the fiery spirit of India’s freedom struggle.
 
• It reflects the passion and determination of Indian leaders and the masses in their fight for independence from British colonial rule.

questions.question: Which of the following crop is NOT associated with dryland farming?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jute**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dryland farming** refers to agricultural practices in regions with limited rainfall, typically less than 500 mm annually. Crops cultivated under dryland farming are drought-resistant and require minimal water.
 
• **Jute** is not associated with dryland farming because it requires a humid climate with high rainfall (typically above 1500 mm annually) for proper growth. It thrives in regions with adequate water supply and is primarily grown in areas like West Bengal, Bihar, and Assam.
 
• **Guar**, also known as cluster bean, is a drought-resistant crop widely grown in arid and semi-arid regions, making it suitable for dryland farming.
 
• **Bajra** (pearl millet) is a staple dryland crop grown in regions with low rainfall. It is heat- and drought-tolerant, making it ideal for dryland farming.
 
• **Ragi** (finger millet) is another dryland crop known for its resilience to drought and ability to grow in poor soils with minimal water requirements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Jute:**

 
 
• **Climate:** Jute requires a warm and humid climate with temperatures between 24°C to 37°C and annual rainfall of 1500-2500 mm.
 
• **Uses:** Jute is primarily used for making ropes, mats, sacks, and other eco-friendly products.
 
• **Major growing regions:** It is cultivated mostly in eastern India, including states like West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, and Assam.
 
• **Harvesting:** Jute is harvested during the rainy season, and its cultivation is dependent on adequate water availability.
 
 
 
• **Dryland Farming:**
 
 
• **Definition:** Dryland farming refers to agricultural practices in areas with low rainfall and no irrigation facilities. It relies on moisture conservation techniques.
 
• **Crops:** Common crops include millet (bajra), sorghum, ragi, pulses, and oilseeds such as mustard and groundnut.
 
• **Regions:** Dryland farming is prevalent in arid and semi-arid regions such as Rajasthan, Gujarat, Karnataka, and parts of Maharashtra.
 
• **Techniques:** Farmers adopt techniques such as contour plowing, mulching, and planting drought-resistant crop varieties to conserve soil moisture.
 
 
 
• **Guar:**
 
 
• **Scientific name:** Cyamopsis tetragonoloba.
 
• **Uses:** Guar is used in food industries as a thickener and stabilizer. Its gum is also used in oil and gas extraction.
 
• **Location:** Guar is widely grown in Rajasthan and Haryana due to its drought resistance.
 
 
 
• **Bajra:**
 
 
• **Scientific name:** Pennisetum glaucum.
 
• **Uses:** Bajra is rich in nutrients and is used in making various traditional foods such as rotis.
 
• **Location:** It is commonly cultivated in dry regions like Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Maharashtra.
 
 
 
• **Ragi:**
 
 
• **Scientific name:** Eleusine coracana.
 
• **Uses:** Ragi is a highly nutritious cereal crop used for making porridge, bread, and malt.
 
• **Location:** It thrives in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Andhra Pradesh, particularly in dry areas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Dryland farming in India:**

 
 
• It accounts for nearly **40% of the total cultivated area** in India.
 
• Dryland areas contribute significantly to the production of **millets, pulses, and oilseeds**.
 
• Regions such as **Rajasthan**, **Maharashtra**, and parts of **Gujarat** are prominent for dryland agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in dryland farming:**
 
 
• **Water scarcity:** Lack of irrigation facilities makes crop cultivation challenging.
 
• **Low yields:** Dryland crops often have lower yields compared to irrigated crops.
 
• **Soil erosion:** Wind and water erosion can degrade soil quality in dry regions.
 
 
 
• **Government initiatives:**
 
 
• **National Mission on Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA):** Aimed at promoting sustainable farming practices in dryland areas.
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana (PMKSY):** Focuses on water conservation and efficient irrigation to support dryland farming.

questions.question: What was the main purpose of land reforms in India post independence?

options.text: To change in the ownership of landholdings.
To increase foreign direct investment in agriculture.
To sell all the landholdings to private companies for better compliance.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To change in the ownership of landholdings**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The main purpose of land reforms in India post-independence was to bring about **equitable ownership of land** by redistributing land from large landholders to landless farmers and tenants.
 
• Land reforms aimed at addressing the issue of **concentration of land** in the hands of a few wealthy individuals, thereby reducing inequality and ensuring social justice.
 
• These reforms included measures like **abolition of zamindari system**, tenancy reforms, and ceilings on landholdings to prevent excessive accumulation of land by individuals. 
 
• The focus was on **empowering small and marginal farmers** and ensuring their access to agricultural land to improve their socio-economic conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Abolition of Zamindari System:**

 
 
• This was one of the earliest measures taken post-independence to eliminate the intermediary system of zamindars who collected revenue on behalf of the British.
 
• The **Zamindari Abolition Act** was implemented in various states to transfer ownership rights to the tillers of the land.
 
• It marked a significant step towards reducing feudal practices and empowering cultivators. 
 
 
 
• **Tenancy Reforms:**
 
 
• Tenancy reforms aimed at securing the rights of tenants by providing protection against arbitrary eviction and granting ownership rights in some cases.
 
• Measures like **fixation of fair rent** and **prohibition of subletting** were introduced to safeguard tenant farmers.
 
• In states like West Bengal and Kerala, tenancy reforms significantly improved the socio-economic status of tenant farmers. 
 
 
 
• **Ceilings on Landholdings:**
 
 
• Land ceiling laws were enacted to limit the maximum land an individual or family could own, and surplus land was redistributed among landless individuals.
 
• The surplus land was allocated to marginalized groups, including **Scheduled Castes (SCs)** and **Scheduled Tribes (STs)**.
 
• This policy aimed at reducing inequality and ensuring equitable distribution of resources. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:**

 
 
• Land reforms were introduced as a part of India's social and economic policies post-independence to address the issues of rural poverty and inequality.
 
• The **First Five-Year Plan (1951-56)** emphasized land reforms as a key strategy for rural development. 
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Provisions:**
 
 
• The **Ninth Schedule** of the Indian Constitution was introduced to safeguard land reform laws from judicial review.
 
• Articles like **Article 39(b) and (c)** of the Directive Principles of State Policy underline the importance of equitable distribution of resources.

• This initiative aimed to improve the status of children in areas such as health, education, nutrition, and protection by ensuring adequate resources and monitoring their utilization.
 
• It was part of broader efforts to meet India's commitments to international conventions

questions.question: Which of the following deficit includes only such transactions that affect the current income and expenditure of the government?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Revenue deficit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Revenue deficit** includes transactions that affect the current income and expenditure of the government. It shows the shortfall in revenue receipts compared to revenue expenditure during a fiscal year.
 
• Revenue deficit is calculated as: **Revenue Expenditure - Revenue Receipts**. It highlights the inability of the government to meet its regular operational expenses from its revenue.
 
• Revenue deficit indicates that the government is unable to cover its day-to-day expenses like salaries, subsidies, and interest payments from its income sources such as tax and non-tax revenues.
 
• This deficit is significant as it reflects the government's reliance on borrowings to finance its routine expenditures, which is not sustainable in the long term.
 
• In contrast to other deficits such as fiscal or trade deficits, revenue deficit focuses exclusively on the revenue aspect of government finances, excluding capital expenditures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Primary Deficit:**

 
 
• It is calculated as: **Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payments**.
 
• Primary deficit shows how much of the government's borrowings are going towards meeting the current year's expenses, excluding interest payments on previous borrowings.
 
• It reflects the government's capacity to manage its finances excluding the burden of past debt.
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:**
 
 
• It is the difference between the total expenditure and total revenue (excluding borrowings) of the government.
 
• Fiscal deficit reflects the total borrowing requirement of the government to bridge the shortfall in its finances.
 
• It includes both revenue and capital expenditures, unlike revenue deficit which only considers current income and expenditure.
 
 
 
• **Trade Deficit:**
 
 
• A trade deficit occurs when a country's imports exceed its exports during a specific time period.
 
• It is calculated as: **Value of Imports - Value of Exports**.
 
• Trade deficit is not related to government finances but rather to the external trade position of a country.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Revenue Deficit:**
 
 
• High revenue deficit indicates fiscal stress as it implies that the government is borrowing not for asset creation but for meeting its operational expenses.
 
• Sustained revenue deficits can lead to a rising debt burden and reduced fiscal flexibility.
 
• Reducing revenue deficit is crucial for achieving fiscal sustainability and maintaining economic stability.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Indian Context:**

 
 
• The **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003** aims to reduce revenue deficit and fiscal deficit in India.
 
• As per the **Union Budget 2023-24**, India has been focusing on reducing its revenue deficit through better tax collection mechanisms and rationalized subsidies.
 
• The government has also emphasized capital expenditure over revenue expenditure to promote long-term economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Global Examples:**
 
 
• Many developed economies, like the **USA and Japan**, often run high fiscal and revenue deficits due to large-scale welfare programs and defense spending.
 
• In contrast, countries like **Germany** maintain low revenue deficits due to disciplined fiscal policies and robust economic management.

questions.question: How is air initially filtered when it is taken into the human body?

options.text: By fine hair in the nostrils

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By fine hair in the nostrils.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Fine hair in the nostrils** acts as the first line of defense in filtering out dust, dirt, and other particulate matter when air enters the respiratory system. These hairs trap larger particles, ensuring cleaner air reaches the respiratory tract.
 
• The nostrils and nasal cavity are lined with **mucus membranes** that produce mucus. This mucus works alongside the nasal hairs to trap smaller particles like pollen, bacteria, and pollutants.
 
• The nasal passages have a moist environment that helps in humidifying the air, which is essential for optimal functioning of the lungs and prevents dryness in the respiratory tract.
 
• **Air filtration** in the nostrils is the first step in the respiratory process, protecting deeper parts of the system such as the throat, trachea, and lungs.
 
• This mechanism ensures that the air entering the body is conditioned to be cleaner and more suitable for the intricate gas exchange process in the lungs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tonsils:**

 
 
• Tonsils are lymphatic tissues located at the back of the throat and do not play a role in air filtration. They are involved in **immune response** and help protect against infections by trapping bacteria and viruses.
 
• While they contribute to overall immunity, their primary function is not related to air filtration, making this option incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Rings of cartilage:**
 
 
• These rings are found in the trachea (windpipe) and provide structural support to keep the airway open for air passage.
 
• They do not perform filtration but ensure that air can flow freely to the lungs without obstruction. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Lungs:**
 
 
• Lungs are the primary organs for gas exchange and oxygenation of the blood, but they are not involved in filtration of air.
 
• Air reaching the lungs has already undergone filtration in the upper respiratory tract (nostrils and nasal passages). This makes this option incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Respiratory System Overview:**
 
 
• The respiratory system is composed of the nostrils, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs. Each part has a specific function.
 
• The nasal cavity, with its hair and mucus, plays the most significant role in initial air filtration.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Nasal Hair:**

 
 
• Found at the entrance of the nostrils, these hairs are short and coarse, designed to trap larger pollutants and particulate matter.
 
• They act as the body's natural filtration system, reducing exposure to harmful airborne particles.
 
 
 
• **Mucus:**
 
 
• Produced by the mucus membranes, mucus acts as a sticky trap for smaller particles like bacteria, pollen, and viruses.
 
• It also keeps the nasal passages moist, preventing dryness and irritation.
 
 
 
• **Cilia:**
 
 
• Microscopic hair-like structures in the respiratory tract move mucus and trapped particles toward the throat, where they can be swallowed or expelled.
 
• Cilia work in coordination with nasal hair and mucus to ensure thorough filtration of air.

questions.question:
What of the following statement is correct regarding phloem of a plant?

I. The translocation in phloem is achieved by utilizing energy.

II. Material are transferred into phloem tissue using energy from ATP.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement I:** The translocation in phloem is achieved by utilizing energy.

 
 
• The process of translocation in the phloem involves the movement of food, primarily in the form of sucrose, from source tissues (like leaves) to sink tissues (like roots, fruits, and seeds).
 
• This process is energy-dependent and occurs with the help of active transport.
 
• Energy from ATP is used to load sucrose into the phloem sieve tubes at the source, creating a high concentration of solutes.
 
• This, in turn, causes water to flow into the sieve tubes by osmosis, generating a pressure gradient that drives the flow of sap. *Hence, Statement I is correct.*
 
 
 
• **Statement II:** Materials are transferred into phloem tissue using energy from ATP.
 
 
• The process of loading materials, particularly sucrose, into the phloem tissue occurs through active transport.
 
• Specialized companion cells in the phloem use ATP to actively transport sucrose into the sieve tube elements against the concentration gradient.
 
• This ensures that the phloem sap contains a high concentration of sucrose, facilitating its movement to other parts of the plant. *Hence, Statement II is correct.*
 
 
 
• As both statements I and II are correct, the correct option is **Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Phloem Structure:**

 
 
• Phloem is a vascular tissue in plants responsible for the transport of organic nutrients, particularly sucrose, from the source (leaves) to sink (roots, fruits, and other storage organs).
 
• It consists of four main components: sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem fibers, and phloem parenchyma.
 
• The sieve tube elements are the main conducting cells, while the companion cells assist in the loading and unloading of materials.
 
 
 
• **Phloem Transport Process:**
 
 
• The movement of solutes in the phloem is called translocation.
 
• It follows the pressure-flow hypothesis, which states that osmotic pressure generated by solute loading and unloading drives the flow of the phloem sap.
 
• Water enters the sieve tubes at the source due to the high osmotic pressure created by the presence of sugars, generating turgor pressure that pushes the sap towards the sink tissues.
 
 
 
• **Energy Dependency:**
 
 
• Unlike xylem transport, which is passive and relies on transpiration pull, phloem transport is an active process that requires energy in the form of ATP.
 
• Active transport is crucial for loading sugars into the sieve tubes at the source and unloading them at the sink.
 
 
 
• **Key Functions of Phloem:**
 
 
• Phloem primarily transports organic nutrients like sucrose, amino acids, and hormones.
 
• It plays a vital role in plant growth and development by distributing the products of photosynthesis to various parts of the plant.
 
• Phloem also facilitates communication within the plant by transporting signaling molecules.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Difference Between Xylem and Phloem:**

 
 
• **Xylem:** Transports water and minerals from roots to aerial parts of the plant. It operates via passive transport and does not require energy.
 
• **Phloem:** Transports organic nutrients like sucrose from source to sink. It requires energy in the form of ATP for active transport.
 
 
 
• **Pressure-Flow Hypothesis:**
 
 
• This widely accepted model explains the movement of substances in the phloem.
 
• It involves the creation of a pressure gradient between the source (high pressure) and the sink (low pressure).
 
• The pressure gradient drives the flow of sap, ensuring efficient distribution of nutrients.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Phloem Transport:**
 
 
• Ensures the proper distribution of nutrients required for growth, development, and storage.
 
• Plays a crucial role in plant repair and defense by supplying energy-rich compounds to damaged or infected areas.
 
• Facilitates the hormonal signaling necessary for coordinating various physiological processes.

questions.question: According to Jaina ethics, the vow of ’aparigraha’ refers to ______.

options.text: non-possession of things more than one’s requirement

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**non-possession of things more than one’s requirement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Aparigraha** is one of the core ethical principles in **Jainism**. It refers to the practice of **non-attachment** or **non-possession of materialistic things** beyond what is necessary for an individual’s needs.
 
• This vow focuses on the idea of living a life of **minimalism** and refraining from accumulating excessive wealth or possessions, which can lead to greed and attachment.
 
• The concept of Aparigraha teaches that material possessions are temporary and can distract individuals from achieving spiritual growth and liberation (**Moksha**).
 
• It encourages individuals to cultivate a mindset of **contentment** and to avoid desires that lead to attachment and suffering.
 
• This principle is not limited to material possessions but also extends to non-material attachments, such as relationships, emotions, and power.
